Southeast: younger, softer sedimentary rocks (chalk, clay); flatter relief; e.g. London Basin, East Anglia.
Diagonal line dividing UK between upland west/north and lowland south/east; reflects geological boundary.
Last Ice Age (until c.10,000 years ago) shaped uplands with U-shaped valleys, corries, ribbon lakes.

walkthroughs.body_html:
The Changing Landscapes of the UK — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

The Changing Landscapes of the UK brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with The Changing Landscapes of the UK.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which line divides upland and lowland Britain?
options: Watford Line
Tees-Exe Line
Hadrian's Wall
Severn-Trent Line

mcqs.q: Where are softer sedimentary rocks found in UK?
options: Scottish Highlands
Southeast England
Snowdonia
Lake District

mcqs.q: Is the UK's pattern of uplands and lowlands random?
options: Uplands are piles of soil left by medieval builders.
Humans are legally barred from altering landscapes.
Where hills and plains occur in the UK has no underlying explanation.
No — older, harder igneous and metamorphic rocks dominate the north and west uplands, while younger, softer sedimentary rocks underlie the south-eastern lowlands; geology controls relief.

mcqs.q: Are UK landscapes shaped only by processes operating today?
options: Only today's rivers, waves and weather have shaped what we see.
UK landscapes were designed in Victorian times.
No — glaciation during past ice ages carved much of the upland scenery, and past tectonic and climatic conditions set the framework that rivers and waves now modify.
Uplands are piles of soil left by medieval builders.

mcqs.q: Do humans play only a minor role in changing UK landscapes?
options: No — farming, forestry, quarrying, settlement and coastal management have transformed most UK landscapes, altering rates of erosion, deposition and drainage.
UK landscapes were designed in Victorian times.
Humans are legally barred from altering landscapes.
UK scenery is almost entirely natural and untouched.
